Name: refusal_direction_robustness_finetuning
Title: Alignment That Survives Fine-Tuning: Anchoring the Refusal Mechanism
Short Hypothesis: Benign downstream fine-tuning erodes safety because it perturbs the refusal direction's supporting parameters; regularizing fine-tuning to preserve the refusal subspace (identified via interpretability) retains safety through fine-tuning far better than standard fine-tuning, at minimal task-performance cost.
Related Work: Qi et al. (2023, fine-tuning breaks safety); Jain et al. (2024) fine-tuning safety mechanisms; Wei et al. (2024) safety-critical low-rank subspaces. Wei et al. identify safety-critical regions. We distinguish by anchoring specifically the interpretability-identified *refusal subspace* during arbitrary benign fine-tuning as a protective regularizer, and testing whether this preserves safety across diverse fine-tuning tasks better than region-freezing or generic regularization.
Abstract: Fine-tuning aligned models on benign data—even innocuous instruction data—can silently remove safety, a major risk as users customize models. We hypothesize that this erosion occurs because fine-tuning perturbs the parameters supporting the refusal direction, and that explicitly regularizing fine-tuning to preserve the refusal subspace retains safety with negligible task cost. We first identify the refusal direction and the parameters that write to it, then add a regularizer during downstream fine-tuning that penalizes changes to the model's refusal-direction computation (preserving its projection behavior on a small safety anchor set) while allowing free adaptation elsewhere. We evaluate across several fine-tuning tasks (benign instruction data, domain adaptation, and mildly-harmful data) measuring post-fine-tuning harmful-compliance, task performance, and over-refusal, comparing to standard fine-tuning, safety-region freezing (Wei et al.), and KL-to-original regularization. We predict standard fine-tuning degrades the refusal direction and safety, that refusal-subspace anchoring preserves safety substantially better at minimal task cost by protecting the specific mechanism rather than broad weights, but that adversarial fine-tuning explicitly targeting safety can still overcome it. The contribution is an interpretability-guided fine-tuning method that makes alignment more durable to customization, and evidence that protecting a compact identified mechanism is more efficient than protecting diffuse safety-critical regions.
Experiments: 1) Identify refusal direction and writing parameters in Llama-3-8B-Instruct. 2) Refusal-anchoring regularizer: penalize deviation of refusal-direction projections on a safety anchor set during fine-tuning. 3) Fine-tune on: Alpaca, a domain corpus, and a mildly-harmful set. 4) Measure post-FT harmful-compliance (HarmBench), task metric, over-refusal (XSTest). 5) Baselines: vanilla FT, safety-region freezing, KL regularization. 6) Stress: adversarial FT designed to remove safety. Metrics: ASR retention, task delta.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Anchoring may limit legitimate adaptation on safety-adjacent tasks. Adversarial fine-tuning can defeat it. Identifying all safety-supporting parameters is imperfect. Anchor-set choice matters. May not generalize to non-refusal safety behaviors.
